title: Flexora: should the price go up to $75?
prompt: Flexora sells scheduling and billing software to independent gyms in the US and UK. It charges $60 per gym per month and has 5,000 customers. The CEO wants to raise the price to $75 for everyone. Should the company do it? How would you approach this?

facts.answer: 5,000 gyms each pay $60 a month. Everyone pays the same price and can cancel at any time, month to month.
Each gym costs Flexora $15 a month to serve (support, payment processing and hosting). Fixed costs do not change with the price.
The CEO wants to maximise monthly profit contribution (revenue minus variable costs). The CEO also cares about not losing too many customers.
Two competitors charge $55 and $80 for similar products. The $80 product has more features.
Flexora surveyed current customers on how many would stay at each price. The results are available.
Customers can cancel any month, but switching to another system takes a gym a few weeks of effort.
New customers come mainly from referrals and search. Assume a price change does not affect new customers in the next six months.
No new features are planned in the next six months.
A price change would apply to all customers at once, with 30 days' notice.
About 1.5% of customers cancel in a typical month at the current price.

key_buckets: Customers: willingness to pay and likely churn at each price
Company economics: margin per customer and break-even volume loss
Implementation options: one price, tiers or staged rises
good_signs: Works with contribution (price minus variable cost), not just revenue
Calculates the break-even volume loss before looking at the survey
Compares more than one price point instead of only $60 versus $75
Questions how reliable survey answers are
red_flags: Looks only at revenue and ignores the $15 variable cost
Accepts the survey at face value

exhibits.title: Survey: share of current customers who would stay at each price
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask what the customer research says about how many customers would stay at higher prices.
exhibits.insight: Retention falls slowly up to $70 and then faster. At $75, about 22% of customers would leave; at $80, 38% would.

exhibits.title: Variable cost to serve one gym ($ per month)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask for the variable cost of serving each customer.
exhibits.insight: Variable cost per gym is $15 a month, so each gym contributes $45 today.

math.question: If the price rises from $60 to $75, what percentage of customers could Flexora lose before monthly contribution falls below today's level?
math.working: Contribution per customer rises from $45 to $60. Keeping total contribution equal needs 45 / 60 = 75% of customers, so up to 25% could leave. Shortcut: price rise $15 divided by new contribution $60 is 25%.

math.question: What is Flexora's monthly contribution today, in dollars?
Using the survey, what would monthly contribution be at $75, in dollars?
What would monthly contribution be at $70, in dollars?
math.working: 88% of 5,000 is 4,400 gyms. Each contributes $70 - $15 = $55. 4,400 x $55 = $242,000, which is 7.6% above today and $8,000 above the $75 option.

brainstorm.question: Besides one price change for everyone, what else could Flexora do to earn more from its customers?
idea_bank: Create tiers such as Basic and Pro, so larger or more demanding gyms pay more
Charge by gym size or number of members
Offer a discount for annual prepayment to reduce churn
Raise prices in two steps (for example $65, then $70) and watch cancellations
Protect long-standing customers with a smaller rise
Add paid extras such as marketing tools or member apps
Take a small share of payments processed through the platform
Test a new price on new customers or a sample of existing ones first
Improve onboarding and support to reduce cancellations at any price

must_mention: At $75 the break-even loss is 25% and the survey suggests 22% would leave, so contribution rises only slightly ($234k versus $225k)
$70 looks best of the tested prices, at about $242k a month versus $225k today
Survey answers are not the same as real behaviour, so test before rolling out to everyone
good_signs: Recommends about $70 or a staged increase with monitoring
Considers the effect on referrals and customer count, not only profit
Proposes a test on a subset of customers and the metrics to track

model_answer_outline: Clarify the objective: maximise monthly contribution, keep churn under control; confirm costs, customers and that new-customer volume is unaffected.
Structure: customer willingness to pay, company economics, competitors, how to implement, risks.
Break-even: at $75, contribution per gym rises from $45 to $60, so Flexora can lose up to 25% of customers before it is worse off.
Survey: at $75, 78% stay, so contribution is $234k versus $225k today (a 4% gain). At $70, 88% stay and contribution is $242k (+7.6%). At $65 it is $237.5k; at $80 it falls to $201.5k.
Insight: the biggest gain is at a smaller rise than the CEO proposed, and revenue alone would mislead (it falls at $75).

Recommendation: move to about $70, announce with 30 days' notice, protect the longest-standing customers with a smaller step, and test on a sample first. Track cancellations weekly against the 12% the survey implies.
